The majority voted against [Labor amendments](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2017-10-25.16.1), which means they were unsuccessful. The amendments concerned people who earn less than $87,000 per year and would have lessened the Medicare Levy they have to pay under these bills. ### What do these bills do? This package of bills will fund the Commonwealth’s contribution to the National Disability Insurance Scheme by, for example, increasing the Medicare levy from 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent of a person’s taxable income. Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd046).

The speaker opposed the Medicare levy increase for Australians earning under $87,000, arguing it would raise taxes on over seven million low- and middle-income workers while the government cuts corporate taxes. They proposed the increase should apply only to those earning above $87,000 and stated the NDIS is fully funded without needing the levy.

The speaker argued that the coalition government is fully funding the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) through a Medicare levy increase of 0.5% to 2.5% from 1 July 2019, expected to raise $3.6 billion in 2019-20 and $4.3 billion in 2020-21. The speaker stated that low-income earners remain exempt, the levy is about $1 per day for average earners, and the previous Labor government left a $4 billion annual funding gap.

The speaker argued for passing the Medicare Levy Amendment (NDIS Funding) Bill 2017, which would increase the Medicare levy by 0.5% to fund the National Disability Insurance Scheme. They named local disability champions including Brad Rossiter, Lauren Ball, Jackie Kay, Luke Stojanovic, and Brent Peter Kelly, and cited that the NDIS will support 460,000 Australians under 65 with permanent disability, with an estimated extra $3.4 billion in services needed.

The speaker supported the Medicare Levy Amendment (National Disability Insurance Scheme Funding) Bill 2017, which raises the Medicare levy from 2% to 2.5% from 1 July 2019 to fully fund the NDIS, citing projected Commonwealth expenditure of $10.8 billion by 2019-20 and a claimed $55.7 billion funding shortfall left by Labor. The speaker noted exemptions for low-income earners and urged Labor to back the measure.

The speaker argued that the Medicare levy increase from 2% to 2.5% in 2019 is necessary to fully fund the NDIS, criticised Labor for repeatedly changing their funding position and leaving a $55.7 billion shortfall, and highlighted Youngcare and clients like Nick and Shevaune as examples of why secure funding is needed.

The speaker argued in support of the Medicare Levy Amendment (National Disability Insurance Scheme Funding) Bill 2017, which increases the Medicare levy from 2% to 2.5% from July 2019 to fully fund the NDIS, criticising the opposition for failing to fund the scheme while in government. They noted the scheme covers 460,000 Australians with disabilities and highlighted the $60 billion annual contribution of 2.7 million unpaid carers.

The speaker argued that the Medicare Levy Amendment (National Disability Insurance Scheme Funding) Bill 2017 is a necessary extension of Labor's own 2013 policy, citing that the NDIS currently costs $5.3 billion and is projected to reach $10.8 billion by 2019–20, with a $55 billion funding gap confirmed by Treasury. They criticised Labor for opposing the bill despite previously supporting a 0.5% Medicare levy increase to fund the scheme, and rejected Labor's claim that the NDIS was fully funded when they left government.

Supported the Medicare Levy Amendment (National Disability Insurance Scheme Funding) Bill 2017, which raises the Medicare levy by half a percentage point, noting Commonwealth NDIS expenditure will reach $5.3 billion in 2017-18 and $10.8 billion by 2019-20, said the coalition inherited a $55.6 billion funding shortfall from Labor, and said the scheme will transform the lives of around 460,000 Australians with disability, including 105,000 in Victoria.

Labor argued that the government's claims Labor did not fully fund the NDIS are false, proposing instead a fairer funding model that raises the Medicare levy only for individuals earning over $87,000 annually and retains the deficit levy for those earning over $180,000, contrasting this with the government's plan which would increase levies on middle- and low-income earners.

The speaker argued that Labor created and will fully fund the National Disability Insurance Scheme, while criticising the government's proposed Medicare levy increase as unfair to low- and middle-income earners and falsely presented as a locked box for NDIS funding. They noted the government’s $65 billion company tax cut and stated Labor’s alternative would raise $4 billion more by increasing the levy on incomes over $87,000 and keeping the deficit levy on incomes over $180,000.

The government's proposed 0.5% Medicare levy increase for all incomes above $21,000 unfairly burdens low-income Australians, while the government could instead fund the NDIS by forgoing $65 billion in corporate tax cuts. Labor would only apply the increase to incomes above $87,000, and the speaker accused the coalition of economic incompetence, citing deficits of $38 billion and $29 billion and national debt of half a trillion dollars.

The speaker opposed the Medicare levy increase from 2% to 2.5% to fund the NDIS, arguing it unfairly taxes workers earning under $87,000 per year. They proposed Labor's alternative of raising the levy only for those earning over $87,000 and reinstating the deficit levy for incomes over $180,000.

The speaker opposed the Medicare Levy Amendment (NDIS Funding) Bill 2017, arguing it would increase taxes for over seven million workers earning less than $87,000 while giving a $65 billion tax cut to big business, and cited cuts of $37.1 million to James Cook University and $30.1 million to Central Queensland University. They supported Labor’s alternative plan to raise more than $4 billion by increasing the Medicare levy only for those earning over $87,000 and keeping the deficit levy on incomes over $180,000.

The speaker opposed the Medicare Levy Amendment (NDIS Funding) Bill 2017, arguing it unfairly raised taxes on low- and middle-income Australians—such as $275 extra for a worker earning $55,000 or a hike for those on $21,000—while cutting taxes for millionaires and big business. They called the NDIS already fully funded and accused the government of undermining Medicare, citing the Medicare freeze and $122 million wasted on a postal survey.

The speaker argued that the government's proposed increase to the Medicare levy on workers earning under $87,000 is unfair and should be rejected, proposing instead to raise the levy only on the top two tax brackets and make the deficit levy permanent—a plan that would raise $4 billion more over 10 years than the government's. The speaker also stated that the NDIS is fully funded from existing savings and accused the government of cutting taxes for millionaires ($16,400 each) and corporations ($80 billion) while forcing low-income Australians to pay more.

The speaker opposed the Medicare Levy Amendment (National Disability Insurance Scheme Funding) Bill 2017, arguing it is a tax increase that unfairly hits low-income earners while giving a tax break to those earning over $180,000, and proposed amendments to exempt those earning under $87,000 from the levy increase and retain the deficit levy for high earners.

The speaker argued that the bill raises taxes on middle-income Australians—7 million workers earning under $87,000, including $275 extra for those on $55,000 and $400 for those on $80,000—to fund tax cuts for high earners and corporations, including a $65 billion handout to multinationals and a $16,400 cut for millionaires, while the NDIS is already fully funded. The speaker opposed the bill and supported the amendment moved by the member for McMahon.

This bill would tighten the rules for unions and employer groups to address misconduct found by a royal commission.
It would let the Federal Court ban officials from office, cancel an organisation's registration, and require a public interest check before groups merge.
The automatic disqualification for officials would apply to criminal offences carrying a jail term of five years or more.
Adds serious criminal offences with a minimum five-year prison term to the automatic disqualification rules for officials.
Gives the Federal Court power to stop officials from holding office for breaking industrial laws or being unfit.
Makes it a crime for a disqualified person to still act as an official or influence the organisation.
Allows the Federal Court to cancel an organisation's registration for corruption, repeated law-breaking, or obstructive industrial action.
Lets the Federal Court suspend an organisation's rights or appoint an administrator to fix governance problems.
Introduces a public interest test that must be passed before registered organisations can amalgamate.
Registered employee and employer organisations and their officials.

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2017-10-16.32.3) to the usual second reading motion, which is "that the bill be read a second time". To read a bill for a second time is to agree with its main idea. ### Amendment text > *That all the words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House calls on the Government to:* > > *(1) abandon its support of the decision of the Fair Work Commission to cut penalty rates because it will mean nearly 700,000 Australians will have their take home pay cut by up to $77 a week; and* > > *(2) legislate to prevent the decision from taking effect to stop Australians from having their penalty rates cut".*

The majority voted to agree with the main idea of the bill, which means the House of Representatives can now discuss it in more detail. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets.html). ### What is the bill's main idea? The [bill was introduced to](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5953): * *include certain serious criminal offences as a new category of ‘prescribed offence’ for the purposes of the automatic disqualification regime in relation to registered organisations;* * *establish an offence for a disqualified person to continue to act as an official or in a way that influences the affairs of an organisation;* * *allow the Federal Court to prohibit officials from holding office in certain circumstances or if they are otherwise not a fit and proper person;* * *allow the Federal Court to cancel the registration of an organisation on a range of grounds; allow applications to be made to the Federal Court for a range of other orders;* * *expand the grounds on which the Federal Court may order remedial action to deal with governance issues in an organisation;* * *expressly provide that the Federal Court may appoint an administrator to an organisation or part of an organisation as part of a remedial scheme; and* * *introduce a public interest test for amalgamations of registered organisations.* Learn more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd045).

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017, calling it a rushed, anti-union attack that goes beyond the Heydon royal commission recommendations, and moved to substitute the bill's words with a call for the government to abandon its support for the Fair Work Commission's decision to cut penalty rates—affecting nearly 700,000 Australians by up to $77 a week—and to legislate to prevent that cut from taking effect.

The speaker argued in support of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017, which includes four measures: allowing the Federal Court to disqualify officers of registered organisations for certain offences, cancel or suspend registration for noncompliance or corrupt conduct, appoint administrators for financial misconduct, and requiring a public interest test for amalgamations. The speaker noted Australia ranks 13th on the Corruption Perceptions Index, behind the UK, Canada, and New Zealand, and linked this to findings from the Royal Commission into Trade Union Governance and Corruption.

The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017 would destroy democratic civil society by targeting union rights and allowing the minister to decide who is fit to lead unions, while ignoring real workplace issues like wage theft and worker exploitation. They referenced specific cases including the Oaky North mine lockout by Glencore, the Bendigo hospital Asset Interiors liquidation, and a backpacker's death in Perth, and claimed the bill breaches ILO Convention 87.

The speaker argued in support of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017, citing personal experience of union thuggery and judicial criticisms of the CFMEU’s record of lawbreaking. The bill would introduce a public interest test for union mergers and add disqualification grounds for officials similar to those for company directors, including for serious criminal offences.

The speaker argued the bill empowers the Federal Court, not the government, to deregister unions for repeated lawbreaking, corruption or serious crimes, and criticised the opposition for failing to condemn CFMEU members' threats to rape workers' children, noting the last union deregistration was by Labor's Bob Hawke in 1986.

Labor will vote against the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017, arguing it is an ideological anti-union measure that shifts the burden of proof onto union officers, allows ministerial or third-party intervention, and contravenes ILO Convention 87. The speech cited the government’s past praise of Kathy Jackson and Michael Lawler, criticized the bill for exceeding Heydon royal commission recommendations, and highlighted record low wage growth and over 1.1 million underemployed Australians.

The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017 is a politically motivated attack on unions, not a genuine integrity measure, and called for a national independent commission against corruption to investigate wrongdoing by companies, unions, public servants and politicians. They opposed the bill's provisions allowing union deregistration for industrial action and restricting union mergers, stating it would increase power imbalances and lower wages.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017, arguing it unfairly targets unions and breaches international law (ILO Convention No. 87), while the government fails to address employer noncompliance with wage theft and insecure work. They cited personal experience of union support after their father's death and criticised the bill for imposing obligations on unions that are not applied to corporations.

Labor argued the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017 is an attack on unions without merit, targeting workers' rights while ignoring corporate malfeasance, and should not pass.

Labor opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017, arguing it was a political attack on unions rather than sound policy, imposing harsher penalties on unions than corporations, and lacking proper consultation. The speaker cited specific concerns about reversed onus of proof for union officials, broad deregistration grounds, and the bill targeting a proposed CFMEU, MUA and TCFUA amalgamation.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017, arguing it unfairly targets unions, breaches international law, and imposes harsher penalties than those for corporations, while citing examples of worker exploitation at Myer, 7-Eleven, and Pizza Hut.

The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017 is a political attack on unions and workers, not based on genuine reform. They cited the CUB workers' dispute, the government's contracting of Centrelink call centre jobs offshore, and claimed the bill violates International Labour Organization conventions, while accusing the LNP of prioritising big business over workers.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017, arguing it unfairly targets trade unions beyond recommendations of the Heydon royal commission and violates ILO Convention 87. Specific objections included provisions for easier union deregistration, a public interest test on mergers targeting the CFMEU, MUA and TCFUA, and higher penalties compared to the Corporations Act.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017, arguing it unfairly targets unions by allowing political disqualification of officials, deregistration based on officials' conduct, and a retrospective merger test aimed at blocking the MUA and CFMEU amalgamation, while also contravening international human rights obligations.

The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017 is a politically motivated attack on the trade union movement, specifically targeting the CFMEU, TCF, and MUA, and is inconsistent with international law and workers' rights. They stated the bill would allow the Federal Court to disqualify union officials and cancel registrations, while no equivalent measures exist for corporations, and claimed it aims to break the political opposition of unions.

The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2017 addresses lawlessness in some registered organisations identified by the Heydon Royal Commission, and that it does not impose harsher standards than on corporations, discourage volunteers, or violate international obligations. The bill targets law-breaking behaviour generally, not specific organisations like the CFMEU, and includes a public interest test for mergers.

The majority voted against an [amendment](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Famend%2Fr5869_amend_e05af329-97e2-467c-a8b7-bcc7a6ede9e0%22;rec=0) to the [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5869), which would have created a national regional higher education strategy. ### What was the amendment? Independent MP for Indi [Cathy McGowan](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/indi/cathy_mcgowan), who proposed the amendment, explained that: > *This amendment is designed to create a financial incentive for students to study at regional universities by creating a HELP-debt-repayment-free period for students studying at regional campuses. Under the amendment, regional students would have a HELP-debt-repayment-free period on the units completed at a regional campus until they reach the $56,205 threshold under the government's proposed legislation. Repayments would then continue as per the government's proposed legislation. The HELP-debt-repayment-free period would apply to students attending a campus that receives a Commonwealth Grant Scheme regional loading or that the minister has identified as having an above-average number of students whose home address is at a regional location.*

The speaker moved the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, which increases student contribution amounts by 1.8% per year for four years (cumulative 7.5% by 2021) and introduces a 2.5% annual efficiency dividend on Commonwealth Grant Scheme grants in 2018 and 2019. The bill lowers the HELP repayment threshold to $42,000 income with a 1% initial repayment rate, extends demand-driven sub-bachelor places to public universities, and allocates 7.5% of Commonwealth Grant Scheme funding ($500 million annually) based on institutional performance metrics from 2019.

The Labor member moved to oppose the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would cut nearly $4 billion from university funding, increase student fees and debt, harm teaching and research, and damage Australia's economy. The speech cited specific figures of $3.8 billion in cuts over five years, a 2.5% cut to operating grants, a 7.5% fee increase over four years, and new loan repayment thresholds starting at $42,000, while noting opposition from vice-chancellors including those from the University of Western Australia, RMIT, and the University of Sydney.

The speaker argued in support of the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, defending it as necessary for sustainability and rejecting Labor's characterisation of it as "tinkering at the edges" or a cut. He noted that university funding is increasing from $17 billion to $21 billion, and the bill includes a 1.8% annual increase in the student cost share (cumulative 7.5% by 2021), a $42,000 repayment threshold, and measures for transparency and subdegree support.

The speaker argued that the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 would increase student fees to the highest proportion since Gough Whitlam’s reforms and cut university funding, driven by Liberal Party ideology rather than evidence. He contrasted this with Labor’s past expansions of access, and rejected the claim that students are the principal beneficiaries of university education, citing public benefits and the burdens of increased debt on families, homebuyers, and small business consumers.

The member for Groom supported the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, highlighting a record $16.7 billion investment in higher education, including base funding of $206.7 million for the University of Southern Queensland rising to $239.7 million by 2021, and announced $15 million for up to eight regional study hubs, scholarships of up to $18,000 for regional STEM and health students, and changes to enabling course fees and allocations.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 and supported the opposition’s amendment, arguing the bill would cut university funding by $45.7 million for the University of Wollongong, increase student fees by 7.5 per cent, and lower the income repayment threshold to $42,000.

The member for Lindsay argued that the Turnbull government's proposed cuts to higher education would disproportionately harm Western Sydney, with Western Sydney University set to lose over $98 million in funding over four years—the highest cut of any university in New South Wales. She opposed the bill, citing that 60% of the university's students are first in their families to attend, and accused the Prime Minister of treating Western Sydney as a community unworthy of educational investment.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, which cuts $3.8 billion from universities, including $617 million from New South Wales and $45.7 million from the University of Wollongong, arguing it would worsen inequality and reduce higher education participation in regional Australia.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would cut university funding by 2.5%, increase student fees, and redirect money to corporate tax cuts rather than improving education. Specific concerns included the bill's impact on enabling programs like Murdoch University's OnTrack, which could affect 350+ students in the Rockingham and Peel regions, and warnings from Times Higher Education editor Phil Baty that funding cuts could harm Australia's international university rankings.

The speech argued the higher education demand-driven system needs sustainable funding, supporting the bill’s measures: increasing maximum student contributions by 7.5 per cent by 2021, lowering the HELP repayment threshold to $42,000, applying a 2.5 per cent efficiency dividend to Commonwealth Grant Scheme subsidies in 2018 and 2019, legislating the HEPPP program with a $985 per low-SES student loading, and extending loan eligibility to most permanent residents and New Zealand citizens without Commonwealth subsidies.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would cut $3.8 billion from higher education, increase student contributions from 42% to 46%, lower the HECS-HELP repayment threshold to $42,000, remove Commonwealth supported places for permanent residents and New Zealand citizens, impose a 2.5% funding cut on universities, and raise student fees by 7.5% over four years.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would cut $3.8 billion from universities and $4 billion from the Education Infrastructure Fund, introduce $3,200 fees for enabling courses, and lower the HELP repayment threshold to $42,000, with Western Sydney University set to lose the most funding in New South Wales.

The speaker opposed the Higher Education Support Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would increase student fees by 1.8% per year for four years (total 7.5% from 2021) and cut university funding through a 2.5% efficiency dividend, making education less affordable. The speaker also criticised the government for lacking detail on the proposed voucher system for postgraduate places.

The speaker argued that the Turnbull government's bill cuts $3.8 billion from university funding, lowers the HELP repayment threshold, and raises fees, benefiting corporations with tax cuts while hurting students—especially those from disadvantaged backgrounds. Specific cuts include $401.8 million from Queensland universities and $37.1 million from James Cook University, and the speaker named Coalition frontbenchers like Malcolm Turnbull, Tony Abbott, George Brandis, and Marise Payne as hypocrites who received free university education under Labor.

The speaker opposed mandatory minimum sentences in the Criminal Code Amendment (Firearms Trafficking) Bill 2017, arguing they fetter judicial discretion, lead to unjust or disproportionate sentences, and are inconsistent with Australia's human rights obligations, citing submissions from the Australian Human Rights Commission and criticism from Chief Justice Wayne Martin.

Migration Legislation Amendment (Regional Processing Cohort) Bill 2016

Labor opposed the Migration Legislation Amendment (Regional Processing Cohort) Bill 2016, arguing it would permanently ban visa applications from anyone processed offshore after July 2013, including those in detention, returned to their country, or resettled elsewhere. The speaker argued the bill breached international law, made resettlement harder, and was a cynical political move by the Turnbull government, while calling for third-party resettlement, increased humanitarian intake, and independent oversight of processing facilities.
Veterans’ Affairs Legislation Amendment (Single Appeal Path) Bill 2016

The bill creates a single appeal path for veterans under the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 2004, allowing cost recovery at the Administrative Appeals Tribunal in certain circumstances and imposing a 28-day statutory timeframe for the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Commission to consider new evidence. Labor supports the bill after negotiations with ministers Stuart Robert and Dan Tehan addressed previous flaws.

The Australian Labor Party opposed the Criminal Code Amendment (Firearms Trafficking) Bill 2015, which proposed mandatory minimum sentences of five years and maximum penalties of 20 years or 5,000 penalty units for firearms trafficking, citing its opposition in principle to mandatory minimum sentencing and the bill's previous rejection in February and August 2015. Labor announced it would not support the bill in its present form, contrasting it with its own 2012 proposal to increase the maximum penalty to life imprisonment.
Australian Crime Commission Amendment (National Policing Information) Bill 2015

The speaker supported the merger of CrimTrac into the Australian Crime Commission (ACC) under two bills, effective from 1 July 2016, to unify national criminal intelligence and information capabilities. Labor will refer the bills to a Senate committee for scrutiny, citing privacy concerns and the need for stakeholder input.
Crimes Legislation Amendment (Proceeds of Crime and Other Measures) Bill 2015

The bill amends the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, Criminal Code, Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006, and AusCheck Act 2007 to clarify non-conviction based confiscation, create new false accounting offences with penalties up to 10 years imprisonment, refine drug analogue and manufacture definitions, expand AUSTRAC information access to South Australia’s ICAC, and broaden AusCheck information sharing with law enforcement and national security agencies. Labor supports the bill and will refer it to the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee for scrutiny.
Veterans’ Affairs Legislation Amendment (2015 Budget Measures) Bill 2015

Labor supported schedules 1 and 3 of the Veterans' Affairs Legislation Amendment (2015 Budget Measures) Bill 2015, which enhance the Veterans' Vocational Rehabilitation Scheme and expand war graves powers to repatriate remains from Terendak Military Cemetery, while agreeing to defer schedule 2—streamlining veterans' appeals—for further negotiations in 2016.
Australian Crime Commission Amendment (Criminology Research) Bill 2015

The Australian Crime Commission Amendment (Criminology Research) Bill 2015 merges the Australian Institute of Criminology into the Australian Crime Commission, creating the Crime and Justice Research Centre. Labor supports the merger after securing assurances that the centre will retain independent research capability, access to datasets, and an open access library, and that there will be no job losses or erosion of employment standards.

The bill expands the Veterans' Vocational Rehabilitation Scheme to allow intermediate rate disability pensioners to work up to 20 hours a week without pension reduction and to set a higher minimum pension for special rate participants, creates a single review pathway for original determinations under the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Act, and authorises the repatriation of the remains of eight service dependants buried at Terendak Military Cemetery in Malaysia.
